newsitem.title: UK: Norway bond rally may boost other Nordic bonds.
newsitem.headline: Norway bond rally may boost other Nordic bonds.

text.p: The dramatic outperformance of Norwegian government bonds could prompt investors who missed the action to look for value in other Nordic markets, analysts said on Friday.

Norway's second interest rate cut since Wednesday wiped out the 10-year yield spread for Norwegian government bonds versus German Bunds, which was zero at 1500 gmt against 19 basis points late on Thursday. Both 10-year bonds were yielding about 5.9 percent.
Analysts were divided on whether the Norwegian central bank could cut rates any further in its attempt to lower the value of its petro-currency.
But they agreed that while this particular yield spread had gone as far as it was likely to go, investment opportunities might exist elsewhere in the region.

"The Norwegian rate cuts are good news for other Nordic markets, showing there is easing potential in some of these countries," said Juli Collins-Thompson, economist at Yamaichi International in London.
Collins-Thompson said Sweden offered the best opportunities with scope for bond yield spreads versus Bunds to shorten.

James McKay, international economist at PaineWebber in London, and Nick Stamenkovic, economist at DKB International, agreed Sweden held promise, but at the short end whereas Finland was a better bet for longer term debt.
"For Sweden and Denmark, the longer end of the curve has become rather tight," said McKay.
However, he said a sharp performance would probably come at the shorter end, prompting Swedish yield curve steepening.
He said there was significant scope for a further 25 basis point easing in Swedish interest rates if December CPI data due later this month was positive.

If labour market reforms were agreed in the next few months, the Swedish repo rate could drop to German levels or possibly even below. Collins-Thompson said Norway might see a further 50 basis points come off interest rates, probably in two stages, following Friday's quarter-point move which brought the deposit rate down to 3.25 percent.
She said Norwegian bonds should rally, "but spreadwise, I wouldn't consider going long Norway and short Bunds".
Collins-Thompson said investors who saw a normally illiquid bond like Norway's trade at zero spread versus Bunds might ask why a country like Finland could not approach such a level also.
She said the Finnish yield spread had fallen to 35 basis points from over 60 last month, and might drop to 15 or lower.

Any interest rate cut in Finland could give such a move impetus, she said, but even without such an incentive the 10-year sector looked good value so long as the economic and inflation outlook remained favourable.
Stamenkovic said any more Norwegian rate cuts would generate market fears about the economy overheating since there was no domestic justification for such easing.
He said Sweden was attractive at the shorter end although further out there was more political uncertainty than for Finland because of Sweden's less positive stance on EMU.

He said the sluggishness of the economy and absence of inflationary pressures would push the Riksbank to continue cutting interest rates this year after its aggressive action in this direction in 1996.

McKay said there was market talk about a possible rate cut in Denmark but he was sceptical about this because domestic economic trends were going in the wrong direction, with the threat of inflationary pressures emerging.
